headline: The Fed's broad dollar index was 118.2126 on September 11, up from 117.9127 on September 8; one euro was quoted at 1.1604 dollars

items.title: Foreign Exchange Rates (H.10), week ending September 11, 2026
items.summary: The Federal Reserve Board's weekly H.10 release, published September 14, 2026, lists daily exchange rates for September 8 through 11; the table shows no data for September 7, the Labor Day holiday on the Board's calendar. On September 11 one U.S. dollar was quoted at 153.7100 Japanese yen and 1.3864 Canadian dollars, while one euro was quoted at 1.1604 U.S. dollars and one British pound at 1.3524 U.S. dollars. The broad U.S. dollar index, with January 2006 set to 100, was 118.2126 on September 11, compared with 117.9127 on September 8.
items.meaning: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. The H.10 table quotes most currencies as units per U.S. dollar, so 153.7100 means one dollar cost 153.71 yen; rates marked with an asterisk, including the euro and the pound, are U.S. dollars per currency unit, so 1.1604 means one euro cost 1.1604 dollars. The broad index is a weighted average of the foreign exchange value of the U.S. dollar against the currencies of a broad group of major U.S. trading partners, so a higher reading means a higher weighted-average value of the dollar against that group.

sections.title: One concept to know
sections.text: An exchange rate can be written in either direction, and the two forms are reciprocals. The H.10 table uses both: the yen appears as 153.7100 yen per U.S. dollar, while the euro appears as 1.1604 U.S. dollars per euro. Turning the euro quote around gives 1 divided by 1.1604, or about 0.8618 euros per dollar. Reading a quote in the wrong direction reverses its meaning: a higher dollars-per-euro number means a euro costs more dollars, not that a dollar buys more euros.

methodology: The Daily Economic Brief is written from primary sources only: official statistical releases and central-bank publications that are public domain or carry open reuse terms (Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, Census Bureau, U.S. Treasury, Federal Reserve, Congressional Budget Office, and peer statistical offices). It never reads or restates commercial news articles or headlines. Every figure links to the release it came from with the time the page was read. Sentences are our own plain-English description of public facts. This edition is a bundled sample written on September 14–15, 2026 from a Federal Reserve Board release published September 14, 2026.
